0.0.n: A standard daytime greeting that works in both casual and polite situations.

0.2.n: This is the first part of the name のあ, not the particle の.

0.3.n: This completes the name のあ; it is not a separate word here.

0.4.n: A polite ending used after her name to introduce herself; Japanese leaves out I here.

1.0.n: Refers to the shopping trip or video being discussed.

1.1.n: Marks 今回 as the topic: she is explaining what she did this time.

1.2.n: The name of a Japanese discount retail chain.

1.3.n: Joins Daiso to the next store name in the list.

1.4.n: Part of the store name Standard Products, not a separate description here.

1.6.n: Completes the store name Standard Products.

1.7.n: Adds THREEPPY to the list of stores.

1.8.n: The name of a Japanese lifestyle goods store brand.

1.9.n: A conversational version of という, used to introduce names before お店.

1.10.n: The お makes 店 sound more polite; Japanese does not require a plural ending.

1.11.n: Marks the stores as the places where she did her shopping.

2.0.n: Combines with に to describe the large quantity she bought.

2.1.n: Turns 大量 into a description of how much shopping she did.

2.2.n: An emphatic, informal noun for buying a lot of things at once.

2.3.n: Marks 爆買い as the activity performed with する.

2.4.n: する becomes して, then adds きて, indicating she did the shopping elsewhere and returned; the ending connects onward.

2.6.n: Suggests the purchases are visible to viewers by this point.

2.7.n: Refers to the area near the speaker, shown in the video.

2.8.n: Marks ここ as the location where the purchases are visible.

2.9.n: Short for 見えている, describing things currently in view rather than someone deliberately looking.

2.10.n: Marks the preceding statement as what she thinks.

2.11.n: The plain form of 思う; the following んです makes the overall expression polite and explanatory.

2.12.n: Short for の, adding an explanatory tone before です.

2.13.n: Adds politeness to the explanation formed with ん.

2.14.n: Softly connects to what comes next without necessarily expressing a strong contrast.

3.0.n: Suggests she wants to make good use of having bought all these items.

3.1.n: Links せっかく to ので in the expression せっかくなので.

3.2.n: Introduces the reason for showing the items, with a gentle explanatory tone.

3.4.n: Softens her announcement rather than specifying an exact amount.

3.5.n: Together with つ, forms 一つ, the general expression for one item.

3.6.n: A general counting ending; repeating 一つ gives the sense of handling items individually.

3.7.n: Repeats the first 一つ to form 一つ一つ, meaning each item individually.

3.8.n: Completes the second 一つ in the repeated expression 一つ一つ.

3.9.n: Refers to the items she bought and plans to show.

3.10.n: Marks 商品 as the things she will introduce.

3.11.n: 紹介する becomes 紹介して, adds いく for moving forward through the task, and たい to express wanting.

3.12.n: Links her wish to introduce the items with 思います.

3.13.n: The polite form of 思う; after たいと, it gently presents what she intends to do.

0.tip: Japanese often leaves out I when the speaker introduces themselves with a name plus です.

1.lit: This time, at shops called Daiso and Standard Products and THREEPPY,
1.tip: The final で marks where the shopping happens; the action comes in the next line.

2.lit: In huge quantities, did shopping and came back, and already here are visible, I think, but,
2.tip: してきて shows she went out, did the shopping, and returned before speaking.

3.lit: Since there is this opportunity, a little, one by one, products want to go on introducing, I think!
3.tip: たいと思います is a gentle, polite way to announce what you would like to do.
